extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media scholars, policy analysts, and students interested in news media effects and journalistic practice
extracted.subtask_short: assessing journalism quality and news effects
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria, measurement items, and methodological notes for evaluating news content, journalistic practice (especially critical/soft news), and public reactions (trust, interest, news consumption). Includes survey instruments and operational definitions used to study these phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toward a More Credible Form of Journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible form of journalism "does not ignore official wrongdoing and does not turn the media agenda over to the newsmakers. It would also be one ... that gives proper voice to the newsmakers, pays sufficient attention to what government is doing well, and assesses politicians’ failings by reasonable standards."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guiding standard for newsroom practice: cover wrongdoing but with judgment; include official voices; report government successes as well as failures; evaluate failings by reasonable standards rather than assuming venality or incompetence. Intended to restore trust and renew interest in politics and news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting the Watchdog Role (Judgment and Distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The press must be a watchdog but must have the judgment to "distinguish real abuse from officials’ small errors of judgment and performance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watchdog journalism is valuable but should avoid 'poisoning the well' by overreacting to minor mistakes; exercise proportionality in criticism so the public does not cease trusting media judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative Journalism Standard (time and rigor required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Top-notch investigative journalism requires a great deal of time and effort to determine the validity of a politician’s claim or to prove instances of wrongdoing or ineptitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality investigation needs resources and time that the 24-hour news cycle often does not permit. Shortcuts (relying on quick allegations, adversary quotes, or surface-level claims) are an anti-pattern that reduce credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of 'Attack' or Source-Supplied Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Much negative content is supplied through journalists’ use of sources rather than deep investigation; reporters often turn to adversaries to attack a claim, supplying criticism via counter-claims rather than verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: substituting adversary quotes/counter-claims for independent assessment. Journalists should verify claims and avoid routine reliance on adversarial framing that creates superficial conflict ('attack journalism').

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance vs. Persistent Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The press shows a pronounced tendency to report what is wrong with politics and politicians rather than what is right; this persistent negativity erodes political trust and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial standard implication: balanced public-affairs reporting (covering both problems and successful governance) is preferable for long-term civic engagement and audience building. Excessive negativity may drive audiences away over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter-as-Participant Bias / Minimizing Reporter-Centered Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters increasingly become direct participants, passing sweeping judgments and occupying more airtime relative to newsmakers (example: reporters spoke six minutes for every minute candidates were heard in a campaign coverage sample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer news formats that center newsmakers' words/actions rather than reporters' commentary; minimize reporter-dominant framing that can shift attention away from substantive public affairs content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft News vs Hard News Distinction (content focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft news focuses on specific incidents (crime, fire, accidents, celebrities) and entertainment; hard news focuses on major events and issues affecting the community and country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying stories or designing content, distinguish soft (incident/people-focused, emotional/entertaining) from hard (policy/issue-focused) news genres; audience interest and reaction to tone differ across these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline Test Methodology (measuring tone effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental test administering two versions of each headline (positive vs negative) to randomized respondents to measure which draws more interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings/guidance: negative headlines attracted more interest on average, especially for soft news; for hard news, content mattered more and positive versions sometimes drew slightly more interest. Use randomized headline variations to assess tone effects by topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey Measurement: Interest in Public Affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey item measuring how much attention respondents pay to government and public affairs (options include: 'a great deal', 'quite a bit', 'just some', 'only a little', or 'none'), and a separate dichotomy used in analysis: those who say 'most of the time' vs 'only now and then'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalization for trends: use consistent response categories across waves to track declines/increases in political interest; compare 'most of the time' vs 'only now and then' as key indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of Government Honesty / Trust Metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of trust in government and views about whether 'most government officials are honest' (used to assess changes over time; e.g., proportion believing officials are honest has dropped substantially).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated cross-sectional survey questions (e.g., NES items) to track shifts in trust; analyze alongside macro events (scandals, economy) to interpret fluctuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular News User Classification (operational rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-step questions used to classify 'regular' users: e.g., for national TV news respondents are first asked frequency (nearly every day / a couple times a week / less) and then whether they usually watch most of the news program; respondents answering 'nearly every day' and 'watch most of the newscast' are categorized as regular viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same two-step operationalization to local TV, radio, and internet measures (frequency + attentiveness/length of time) to identify regular consumers vs incidental/exposure-only users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived Tone Adjectives Battery (SN-17)
rubrics_metrics.description: A battery of paired adjectives to assess public perceptions of news (examples: fair/biased, negative/positive, interesting/boring, serious/sensational, informative/uninformative, superficial/thorough, accurate/misleading, depressing/uplifting, enjoyable/not enjoyable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate order of adjectives and scramble items to reduce order effects; use binary forced-choice pairs to capture directional perceptions of the news tone and quality. These perceptions predict attention and satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Values Importance Scale (SN-19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a 5-point scale, respondents rate how important each attribute is when choosing news: 'is lively and enjoyable'; 'fits easily into your daily schedule'; 'is timely and up to date'; 'provides information that helps you to understand public affairs'; 'provides information that helps you in your daily life'; 'tells you about the good things and the bad things that happen to ordinary people'; 'stirs your emotions and feelings'; 'is substantial rather than sensational.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This set of importance items identifies what audiences value (information vs entertainment vs schedule fit); useful for segmenting audiences (e.g., 'busy' people place a premium on public affairs information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft-News Survey Split-Sample Design
rubrics_metrics.description: Questionnaire design note: SN-1 through SN-19 are asked of one-half the sample; SN-20 of one-half of that half; SN-21 of the other one-half of the half (a nested split-sample design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use split-sample designs to limit respondent burden while enabling multiple experiments or modules; document which items are asked to which subsamples for weighting and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization and Caveat for Internet News Use
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey asked whether respondents rely on the Internet for daily news and followed with a question about whether they read material for a reasonable length of time; only 5% qualified as regular Internet news consumers but caution: many Internet 'news' encounters are inadvertent and fleeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret small proportions of self-reported regular Internet news use cautiously; include follow-up attentiveness items (time spent per encounter) to distinguish deep vs incidental consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived Negativity Predicts Reduced Attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey finding used as a criterion: the best predictor of whether people say they are paying 'less' rather than 'more' attention to the news is the perception that today's news is 'negative' rather than 'positive' (among those paying less attention, 93% perceive news to be largely negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing causes of declining news consumption, include perception-of-tone measures because they strongly predict self-reported declines in attention.
